description.text:
Cards given with the monthly magazine CoroCoro Comic from its November 1996 issue to its May 2001 issue, before Japanese promos had collection numbers. The first, a glossy Pikachu, came out on 15 October 1996 together with a Jigglypuff. The magazine's jumbo cards are listed under Miscellaneous Promos.

Many issues after that carried a card or a few: Mewtwo, Surfing Pikachu with the Imakuni? card, Flying Pikachu, Meowth with Computer Error, Gym Leaders' Pokémon such as Brock's Onix and Erika's Dratini, and Hama-chan's Slowking, then Togepi, Marill, Wooper, Cleffa, Scizor, Unown R and Smoochum, and last Shining Mew in the May 2001 issue. Five cards came from CoroCoro's 1999 Best Photo Contest, and the Spring 1999 issue of Hyper CoroCoro gave English prints of Pikachu and Jigglypuff with a gray star.

This photo of two Bulbasaur and an apple was one of CoroCoro's five, with Pikachu, Poliwag, Magikarp and Gyarados, announced in the magazine's August 1999 issue; it has a camera in place of a set symbol, and its bottom edge names it a "Best Photo Contest" prize card.

description.text:
Given with the November 1997 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in October 1997. Toshinao Aoki's Pikachu floats under a bunch of balloons; it has Thundershock and Fly, which spares it from attacks on the next turn unless a coin flip fails, and its text says it can't evolve into Raichu. Its Pokédex text calls it a Pikachu that overcame its weakness by flying.

CoroCoro's December 1998 issue offered it again in a draw for 2,000 readers, with Surfing Pikachu, Jynx, Cubone and Farfetch'd; the reprint can't be told apart from the first print. The 1998 Kamex Mega Battle tournaments counted it among the hard-to-get promos a deck could hold only one copy of. All Nippon Airways gave versions with an airliner added to the picture in 1998 and 1999, and Wizards of the Coast printed this art in English as Black Star promo 25 in 2001.

description.text:
One of the first two Pokémon promo cards: CoroCoro Comic gave it away in mid-October 1996, five days before the Japanese Base Set came out, together with a Jigglypuff. Collectors call it Ivy Pikachu, for the ivy leaves in its art box; Keiji Kinebuchi drew it. It came out several ways: glossy in that CoroCoro issue, crediting Ken Sugimori by mistake; non-glossy and correctly credited in the November 1996 guide "Easily Understand How to Play Pokémon Cards"; and glossy and corrected for the 2,000 winners of a CoroCoro postcard draw in 1998.

A fifth version, the "marketing variation", with an extra pair of leaves under Pikachu's foot, appears in early advertising but was likely never meant to be given out. Wizards printed the art in English as Black Star Promo 1, and an English grey-star copy was given away in Japan in 1999.

description.text: Given with the August 1999 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in July 1999, the same issue as Koga's Ninja Gym. Given with the January 1998 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in December 1997, the same issue as Computer Error. Ken Sugimori's Meowth glows gold, with Team Rocket's R in place of a set symbol; its attacks are Scratch and Pay Day, which draws a card for each heads before a tails, and its Pokédex text says it loves round things and brings home coins it finds on its night outings.

CoroCoro's October 1998 issue offered it again in a draw for 2,000 readers, with Ivy Pikachu, Jigglypuff and Brock's Onix; the reprint can't be told apart from the first print. This art was never printed in English; the Meowth CoroCoro gave in 1999 for the Game Boy card game is a different card.

description.text:
Given with the June 1997 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in May 1997. Benimaru Itoh's Mewtwo crackles with green energy; it has 70 HP and two attacks, Energy Absorption, which takes up to two Energy cards from your discard pile, and Psyburn, and no set symbol. Its Pokédex text says a Pokémon of unheard-of ferocity was born from rearranging Pokémon genes.

CoroCoro's November 1998 issue offered it again in a draw for 2,000 readers, with a Mew, Misty's Staryu and another Mewtwo; the reprint can't be told apart from the first print. Wizards of the Coast printed the same art in English as Black Star promo 14, which came with the North American home video of Pokémon: The First Movie in 2000.

Given with the November 2000 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in October 2000; its bottom line names it the issue's bonus card. Hideki Kazama's Unown is the letter R, and its Pokémon Power, Reassure, removes every damage counter from your Unown in play when it is put onto your Bench from your hand.

description.text:
Given with the September 1999 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in August 1999, for the second Pokémon film, Revelation Lugia (Pokémon: The Movie 2000), which opened in Japan on 17 July 1999. In the film Slowking is voiced by the comedian Masatoshi Hamada of the duo Downtown, "Hama-chan", and the card credits its childlike drawing to Hamada himself. It carries a film logo and the word HAMADA in its lower corner, the star symbol of Neo Genesis, and a bottom line naming it the issue's bonus card.

Its attacks are jokes: こまったなぁ ("what a fix") can only be used after muttering its name three times, and leaves both Active Pokémon Confused; どつく ("whack") does 20 damage, but only after muttering "ee no ka naa" three times. The card was never printed in English.

Given with the September 1997 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out on 15 August 1997. Its picture is a photograph of Imakuni?, the singer who sang and danced the card game's TV commercial song "Pokémon Ierukana?" Played as a trainer, it leaves your own Active Pokémon Confused, and though it shows "HP ?" it can't be put into play as a Pokémon; its text tells readers to greet him with "Imakuni?-san, konnichiwa" if they meet him in town.

The December 1998 Bessatsu CoroCoro Comic special issue offered it again in a draw for 2,000 readers, with Super Energy Retrieval, Computer Error, Lt. Surge's Electabuzz and Erika's Dratini; the reprint can't be told apart from the first print. The 1998 Kamex Mega Battle tournaments counted it among the hard-to-get promos a deck could hold only one copy of. A matte copy was given out at the 1999 International Tropical Mega Battle in Hawaii, and is described on its own variant. Imakuni? came back on later cards in new art, but this one was never printed in English.

description.text:
The matte print of Imakuni?. It was given out at the 1999 International Tropical Mega Battle, held from 24 to 27 August 1999 at the Hilton Hawaiian Village in Honolulu for junior players from the United States and Japan. Imakuni? himself was there, in costume, playing the children with his own "Confusion Deck" and handing out badges with his face on them, and he helped hand out the prizes, among them the matte Exeggutor every player received.

For years nobody knew where the matte card came from. Collectors traced it in 2018 from a copy Imakuni? had signed and dated 25 August 1999, and from players of that event who had kept theirs.

description.text: Given with the August 1999 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in July 1999, the same issue as Giovanni's Nidoking. Koga's Ninja Gym is a Stadium card by Keiji Kinebuchi: a tatami-floored ninja hall with a puff of smoke in the middle, and the Gym symbol. While it is in play, each player may flip a coin once a turn and, on heads, put one of Koga's Basic Pokémon from their deck onto their Bench.

Given with the July 1999 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in June 1999. Ken Sugimori's Marill, one of the new Pokémon of the coming Gold and Silver games, is printed in the original card layout rather than the one the Neo expansions brought in, like the Togepi CoroCoro gave a month earlier, and it carries the star symbol of Neo Genesis. Its one attack is Water Gun, and its Pokédex text says its fur repels water, so it stays fluffy after a swim.

Wizards of the Coast printed this art in English as Black Star promo 29, the Pokémon League promo of December 2000.

description.text: Given as a glossy card with the February 1997 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in January 1997. description.text: The matte print from the JR East Pokémon Stamp Rally of August 1997, the first of many events Japan Railways ran with the Pokémon card game. Participants had two days to visit 30 stations on Tokyo's Yamanote line and fill a stamp book with a different Pokémon stamp at each; all 100,000 advance tickets sold out, and the rally ran from 9 to 17 August 1997. Those who completed the book were given a booklet holding this Mew and a Surfing Pikachu, reprints of CoroCoro promos printed matte instead of glossy.
